title: When the Atlas Sings
premise: In the fog-bound port city of Greyhaven, Coral Okafor has survived by being unremarkable: an apprentice clockmaker with forged papers and a talent for gears. When a census taker flags her documents, she learns the city is purging undocumented residents onto ships bound for penal colonies—unless they can prove kinship to a registered citizen. Coral's found family of misfits must fabricate a lineage, but only one berth on the legitimate registry remains, forcing her to choose between the old clockmaker who raised her craft, the runaway boy she calls brother, and the woman she loves. In the end, Coral sacrifices her own name, registering herself as 'deceased' so the others may live openly—and discovers that a person erased from paper can still be written into memory, as the observatory clock she restored chimes her true name across the city.
about_author: Wendell Ashgrove is the pen name of a former museum conservator who spent a decade restoring maritime instruments before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about people history tried to lose.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Oiled Silence
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She works through the night on the observatory's master clock, establishing her precision, her forged papers hidden in her toolbox, and her careful invisibility among Greyhaven's dockside community. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking constant fear.

chapters.title: A Question of Kin
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Census taker Mr. Pell visits the workshop, asking about her surname, her parents, her arrival year. Her employer, Master Ivo Brandt, covers for her—but Coral notices Pell writing something down anyway. Beat: first crack in her armor.

chapters.title: The Family We Assembled
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter at the boarding house. Introduce the found family: Tam, the runaway boy; Sefa, the herbalist; Old Marta; and Wren, the night-soil cart driver Coral loves. Warmth and banter, undercut by news that a neighbor was taken in the night. Beat: belonging and dread intertwined.

chapters.title: What the Registry Demands
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She reads the new edict aloud: undocumented residents have thirty days to prove citizen kinship or board the transport ship Vespergate. The family realizes none of their bonds exist on paper. Beat: the abstract threat becomes arithmetic.

chapters.title: Master Brandt's Ledger
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She asks Brandt to claim her as kin; he hesitates, revealing he has a estranged daughter whose name he cannot surrender without consequence. He offers instead to teach her the master clock's heart—a gift that feels like an apology. Beat: love complicated by debt.

chapters.title: Paper Daughters
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Sefa proposes forging adoption papers; Tam volunteers to steal a blank registry form from the customs house. Coral resists—forgery is how her real family was destroyed years ago. Beat: survival methods collide with trauma.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Counts Stars
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam scouts the customs house and reveals he can read the stars better than any chart—he learned navigation from his lost father, a sailor. His competence earns him a place in the plan but also makes him visible. Beat: pride shadowed by exposure.

chapters.title: Pell's Second Visit
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Pell returns, softer now, almost kind, hinting that he too has someone to protect. He warns Coral that the Vespergate list is already drafted and her name is on it. Beat: enemy revealed as fellow prisoner of the system.

chapters.title: One Berth, Four Names
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The family counts: one legitimate kinship registration remains available through Marta's late husband's line. Four candidates. Marta refuses to choose; the family fractures into polite, terrible silence. Beat: the central dilemma lands.

chapters.title: Gears Within Gears
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Working inside the master clock, Coral finds a hidden compartment with Brandt's old letters—and evidence the registry system itself was built by men like him, men who once erased others. Beat: history rhymes; rage becomes resolve.

chapters.title: The Auction of Mercy
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. A black-market broker offers extra berths at ruinous prices. The family pools everything; it buys safety for exactly one more person. Now two berths, three claimants. Beat: hope that deepens the wound.

chapters.title: Tam Runs
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Overwhelmed by guilt, Tam attempts to give up his claim and stows away toward the Vespergate voluntarily, believing he's worth least. Coral drags him back from the docks at dawn. Beat: self-worth as the story's hidden battlefield.

chapters.title: What Wren Carries
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confesses she has registered kinship status already—an old marriage certificate from a sham wedding she never dissolved. She could claim anyone. But using it means exposing herself to charges of fraud. Beat: love measured against risk.

chapters.title: The Clockmaker's Confession
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV (first departure). Brandt admits he informed on Coral's parents twenty years ago to save his own workshop—the same choice now facing her. He begs her to take the berth and let him be punished. Beat: the past arrives wearing the present's face.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Days
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Countdown structure: the family prepares papers, goodbyes, contingencies. Small domestic scenes—mending clothes, cooking, teaching Tam constellations—while the deadline ticks like the clock Coral tends. Beat: tenderness under sentence.

chapters.title: The Form in the Rain
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The forgery attempt fails; Pell intercepts Tam at the customs house but lets him go, whispering that he's counting on Coral to do 'the arithmetic.' The family realizes Pell knows everything. Beat: the trap closes gently, which is worse.

chapters.title: Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Alone at midnight in the observatory, Coral works the problem: four people, two berths, one fraud risk. She arrives at the answer she's been avoiding—her own name is the one that can be spent. Beat: cold clarity, terrible peace.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Climax, multiple POVs interwoven. At the registry office, Coral declares herself dead—presenting Brandt's testimony of a fatal workshop accident—and registers Wren as Marta's kin and Tam as Wren's ward. Pell watches, then stamps the pages. Beat: sacrifice performed in broad daylight.

chapters.title: Vespergate Departs
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The transport ship sails with its stolen passengers; Tam watches from the quay, alive and documented, understanding for the first time what being chosen cost. Beat: survivor's grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: A Woman Without Papers
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Officially deceased, Coral hides in the observatory's clock tower. Brandt brings food and, finally, forgiveness—his and hers. She begins repairing not just clocks but the city's forgotten records, becoming a ghost who restores names. Beat: erasure repurposed as vocation.

chapters.title: The Chime at Midnight
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. On the anniversary, the family gathers as the restored master clock strikes twelve—and Coral, hidden in its workings, has rigged the carillon to play a melody her mother sang. The whole city hears a song no register contains. Beat: mourning turned to monument.

chapters.title: When the Atlas Sings
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, coda. Years later, Pell—now retired—visits the tower and leaves a blank registry form and a pen. Coral writes a single word: her true name, kept where no census will ever find it. Beat: identity reclaimed privately; the family endures.
